claim: BehaviorDEPOT is a simple, flexible software program that can detect behavior from video timeseries and can analyze the results of experimental assays.
source: We developed BehaviorDEPOT (DEcoding behavior based on POsitional Tracking), a simple, flexible software program that can detect behavior from video timeseries and can analyze the results of experimental assays.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a description of what was developed.

claim: BehaviorDEPOT calculates kinematic and postural statistics from keypoint tracking data.
source: BehaviorDEPOT calculates kinematic and postural statistics from keypoint tracking data and creates heuristics that reliably detect behaviors.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract describing the software's functionality.

claim: BehaviorDEPOT requires no programming experience.
source: It requires no programming experience and is applicable to a wide range of behaviors and experimental designs.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a feature of the software.

claim: The BehaviorDEPOT freezing detection heuristic achieves above 90% accuracy in videos of mice and rats.
source: Our freezing detection heuristic achieves above 90% accuracy in videos of mice and rats, including those wearing tethered head-mounts.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a performance metric.

claim: The BehaviorDEPOT freezing detection heuristic achieves above 90% accuracy in videos of animals wearing tethered head-mounts.
source: Our freezing detection heuristic achieves above 90% accuracy in videos of mice and rats, including those wearing tethered head-mounts.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a performance metric for a specific experimental condition.

claim: BehaviorDEPOT stores behavioral data framewise for easy alignment with neural data.
source: Behavioral data is stored framewise for easy alignment with neural data.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a feature of the software.

claim: BehaviorDEPOT can analyze fear conditioning assays.
source: We demonstrate the immediate utility and flexibility of BehaviorDEPOT using popular assays including fear conditioning, decision-making in a T-maze, open field, elevated plus maze, and novel object exploration.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a demonstrated application.

claim: BehaviorDEPOT can analyze decision-making in a T-maze.
source: We demonstrate the immediate utility and flexibility of BehaviorDEPOT using popular assays including fear conditioning, decision-making in a T-maze, open field, elevated plus maze, and novel object exploration.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a demonstrated application.

claim: BehaviorDEPOT can analyze open field assays.
source: We demonstrate the immediate utility and flexibility of BehaviorDEPOT using popular assays including fear conditioning, decision-making in a T-maze, open field, elevated plus maze, and novel object exploration.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a demonstrated application.

claim: BehaviorDEPOT can analyze elevated plus maze assays.
source: We demonstrate the immediate utility and flexibility of BehaviorDEPOT using popular assays including fear conditioning, decision-making in a T-maze, open field, elevated plus maze, and novel object exploration.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a demonstrated application.

claim: BehaviorDEPOT can analyze novel object exploration assays.
source: We demonstrate the immediate utility and flexibility of BehaviorDEPOT using popular assays including fear conditioning, decision-making in a T-maze, open field, elevated plus maze, and novel object exploration.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a demonstrated application.

claim: Discrete behaviors represent outward manifestations of cognitive and emotional processes.
source: Discrete behaviors represent outward manifestations of cognitive and emotional processes.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as background knowledge.

claim: It remains a major challenge to quantify naturalistic behaviors in the laboratory in a rapid, reliable, and spatiotemporally precise manner.
source: However, it remains a major challenge to quantify naturalistic behaviors in the laboratory in a rapid, reliable, and spatiotemporally precise manner.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a problem in the field.

claim: Manual behavioral annotation is time-consuming and rife with inconsistency.
source: In most labs, this work is done manually, a time-consuming process that is rife with inconsistency.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a limitation of current methods.

claim: Automated detection of freely moving animal behaviors is faster than manual annotation.
source: Automated detection of freely moving animal behaviors is faster and expands the parameter space that can be explored.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as an advantage of automated methods.

claim: Automated detection can eliminate errors associated with manual annotation such as inter-rater inconsistency.
source: Automated detection can also eliminate errors associated with manual annotation such as inter-rater inconsistency due to insufficient rater training and rater fatigue.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as an advantage of automated methods.

claim: Commercially available software for automated behavior analysis is expensive.
source: Commercially available software for automated behavior analysis is expensive and the underlying algorithms are hidden, which prevents customization or interrogation to determine why a particular result is reported.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a limitation of commercial software.

claim: The underlying algorithms of commercially available behavior analysis software are hidden.
source: Commercially available software for automated behavior analysis is expensive and the underlying algorithms are hidden, which prevents customization or interrogation to determine why a particular result is reported.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a limitation of commercial software.

claim: Commercially available behavior detectors are prone to failure when animals are wearing head-mounted hardware.
source: Moreover, commercially available behavior detectors are prone to failure when animals are wearing head-mounted hardware for manipulating or recording brain activity.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a limitation of commercial software.

claim: Open-source hardware for recording and manipulating neural activity is becoming increasingly available.
source: As open-source hardware for recording and manipulating neural activity become increasingly available (Luo et al., 2018), more labs are integrating optogenetics, miniscopes, fiber photometry and electrophysiological recordings into their behavioral experiments.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to support the claim.

claim: More labs are integrating optogenetics, miniscopes, fiber photometry and electrophysiological recordings into their behavioral experiments.
source: As open-source hardware for recording and manipulating neural activity become increasingly available (Luo et al., 2018), more labs are integrating optogenetics, miniscopes, fiber photometry and electrophysiological recordings into their behavioral experiments.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a trend in the field, with a citation.

claim: Previously established methods use background subtraction and pattern classifiers to estimate animal positions in video timeseries.
source: Previously established methods use techniques including background subtraction and pattern classifiers to estimate animal positions in video timeseries and then abstract animal movement to a center of mass or an ellipse for analysis (Ohayon et al., 2013; Branson et al., 2009; Noldus et al., 2001; Geuther et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: JAABA uses machine learning to classify behaviors based on the outputs of tracking systems.
source: JAABA (Kabra et al., 2013) uses machine learning to classify behaviors based on the outputs of tracking systems such as MotionTracker (MoTr) (Ohayon et al., 2013) and Ctrax (Branson et al., 2009), which fit ellipses to track animal movements.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations.

claim: JAABA requires no coding expertise.
source: JAABA requires no coding expertise and has been widely used in the fly community to report complex behaviors including social interactions and various kinds of locomotion.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation.

claim: JAABA has been widely used in the fly community.
source: JAABA requires no coding expertise and has been widely used in the fly community to report complex behaviors including social interactions and various kinds of locomotion.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation.

claim: Only a few rodent studies have employed JAABA.
source: However, only a few rodent studies have employed JAABA (Sangiamo et al., 2020; Neunuebel et al., 2015; Phillips et al., 2019; Nomoto and Lima, 2015; van den Boom et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations.

claim: Ellipses cannot resolve the detailed spatiotemporal relationships between individual body parts that characterize many complex behaviors.
source: One limitation is that ellipses cannot resolve the detailed spatiotemporal relationships between individual body parts that characterize many complex behaviors.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a limitation of ellipse-based tracking.

claim: Methods that rely on background subtraction are not robust to environmental complexity.
source: Moreover, many methods that rely on background subtraction or similar approaches are not robust to environmental complexity and require behavioral assays that can be performed in an empty arena (Geuther et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation.

claim: Pose estimation algorithms based on machine learning can accurately track individual keypoints on an animal's body.
source: Newer pose estimation algorithms that are based on machine learning can accurately track individual 'keypoints' on an animal's body (e.g. nose, ears, joints) (Mathis et al., 2018; Pereira et al., 2019; Graving et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations.

claim: Keypoint tracking is robust to environmental changes in behavioral arenas.
source: Keypoint tracking is robust to environmental changes in behavioral arenas and the relationships between the locations of keypoints allow researchers to resolve temporal pose sequences with fine detail.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as an advantage of keypoint tracking.

claim: MARS and SimBA use supervised machine learning to classify behaviors based on the positions of keypoints.
source: Recently developed open-source software packages such as MARS (Segalin et al., 2021) and SimBA (Nilsson et al., 2020) use supervised machine learning to classify behaviors based on the positions of keypoints on an animal's body.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations.

claim: Additional rounds of machine learning are computationally-intensive and require significant amounts of human-labeled video data.
source: However, additional rounds of machine learning are computationally-intensive and require significant amounts of human-labeled video data.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a limitation of machine learning approaches.

claim: BehaviorDEPOT comprises six independent modules.
source: BehaviorDEPOT comprises six independent modules that form a flexible, multifunctional pipeline that can run experiments, detect behaviors in video timeseries, and analyze behavioral data (Figure 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1.

claim: BehaviorDEPOT has a graphical interface that accommodates users with no prior coding experience.
source: Its graphical interface accommodates users with no prior coding experience.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a feature of the software.

claim: The Analysis Module imports keypoint tracking data and calculates postural and kinematic metrics.
source: The Analysis Module imports keypoint tracking data, calculates postural and kinematic metrics (e.g. body length, head velocity), uses these data as the basis of heuristic behavior detectors, and analyzes the results of experiments (e.g. report the effects of an optogenetic manipulation during cued fear conditioning).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the Analysis Module.

claim: BehaviorDEPOT provides hard-coded heuristics for detecting freezing, jumping, rearing, escape, locomotion, and novel object exploration.
source: We provide hard-coded heuristics for detecting freezing, jumping, rearing, escape, locomotion, and novel object exploration.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a feature of the software.

claim: BehaviorDEPOT provides analysis functions for the open field test, elevated plus maze, T-maze, and three chamber assays.
source: We also provide analysis functions for the open field test, elevated plus maze, T-maze, and three chamber assays.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a feature of the software.

claim: The Analysis Module generates rich data structures containing spatial tracking data, postural and kinematic data, behavioral timeseries, and experimental parameters.
source: The Analysis Module generates rich data structures containing spatial tracking data, postural and kinematic data, behavioral timeseries, and experimental parameters.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the Analysis Module.

claim: All data in BehaviorDEPOT is stored framewise for easy alignment with neural signals.
source: All data is stored framewise for easy alignment with neural signals.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a feature of the software.

claim: The Experiment Module can run fear conditioning experiments by using Arduinos to control shockers, arenas, and lasers for optogenetics.
source: The Experiment Module can run fear conditioning experiments by using Arduinos to control shockers, arenas, and lasers for optogenetics.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the Experiment Module.

claim: The Analysis Module imports videos and accompanying keypoint tracking data and smooths the tracking data.
source: The Analysis Module imports videos and accompanying keypoint tracking data and smooths the tracking data.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the Analysis Module workflow.

claim: DeepLabCut produces a list of comma-separated values that contains framewise estimates of the X-Y coordinates for designated body parts as well as a likelihood statistic for each estimated point.
source: DLC produces a list of comma-separated values that contains framewise estimates of the X-Y coordinates for designated body parts as well as a likelihood statistic for each estimated point.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing DLC output.

claim: The Analysis Module applies a threshold based on DLC likelihood and performs a Hampel transformation to remove outliers.
source: The Analysis Module applies a threshold based on DLC likelihood and performs a Hampel transformation (Hampel, 1974) to remove outliers.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the Analysis Module processing steps.

claim: A local regression smoothing method (LOWESS) is applied to the tracking data.
source: Then, a local regression smoothing method (LOWESS) is applied to the data (Cleveland, 1981), and sub-threshold tracking values are estimated using surrounding data and spline interpolation (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a citation and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The BehaviorDEPOT freezing heuristic combines a convolution-based smoothing operation with a low-pass velocity filter and applies a minimum duration threshold.
source: The BehaviorDEPOT freezing detection heuristic combines a convolution-based smoothing operation with a low-pass velocity filter and then applies a minimum duration threshold to identify periods of freezing.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the freezing heuristic.

claim: Thresholding the velocity of a midpoint on the back and the angular velocity of the head produced the most accurate freezing detection heuristic.
source: After exploring the predictive value of different keypoints using the Data Exploration Module (described below), we determined that thresholding the velocity of a midpoint on the back and the angular velocity of the head produced the most accurate freezing detection heuristic (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2D.

claim: BehaviorDEPOT freezing detection was highly consistent with human annotations in videos recorded at 50 fps with a high resolution camera.
source: BehaviorDEPOT freezing detection was highly consistent with human annotations (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2F with performance metrics.

claim: The freezing heuristic had precision of 0.86, recall of 0.92, F1 of 0.89, and specificity of 0.97 on videos recorded at 50 fps.
source: (F) Evaluation of freezing heuristic performance on videos recorded at 50 fps with a high resolution, high framerate camera (p=0.95, paired t-test, N=6; Precision: 0.86, Recall: 0.92, F1: 0.89, Specificity: 0.97).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2F caption with statistical analysis.

claim: The freezing heuristic had precision of 0.98, recall of 0.88, F1 of 0.93, and specificity of 0.99 on videos recorded at 30fps with a standard webcam.
source: (G) Evaluation of freezing heuristic performance on videos recorded at 30fps with a standard webcam (p=0.10, paired t-test, N=6; Precision: 0.98, Recall: 0.88, F1: 0.93, Specificity: 0.99).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2G caption with statistical analysis.

claim: Tracking errors less than 4 pixels produced the highest F1 scores in the analysis.
source: A linear regression analysis revealed that tracking error had a significant effect on precision and on the F1 score without affecting recall or specificity (Figure 2—figure supplement 1; Supplementary file 5), with tracking errors <4 pixels producing the highest F1 scores in our analysis.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Freezing behavior is defined as the absence of movement except for respiration.
source: Freezing behavior, defined as the absence of movement except for respiration (Grossen and Kelley, 1972; Fanselow and Bolles, 1979; Fanselow, 1984), is widely studied as a proxy for both learned and innate fear (Anagnostaras et al., 1999; Anagnostaras et al., 2010; Perusini and Fanselow, 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations.

claim: Freezing behavior is widely studied as a proxy for both learned and innate fear.
source: Freezing behavior, defined as the absence of movement except for respiration (Grossen and Kelley, 1972; Fanselow and Bolles, 1979; Fanselow, 1984), is widely studied as a proxy for both learned and innate fear (Anagnostaras et al., 1999; Anagnostaras et al., 2010; Perusini and Fanselow, 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations.

claim: Most labs still score freezing manually or using expensive commercially available software programs.
source: Despite the heavy study of freezing behavior, most labs still score freezing manually or using expensive commercially available software programs that often fail when animals have tethered headmounts.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a problem in the field.

claim: Commercial freezing software often fails when animals have tethered headmounts.
source: Despite the heavy study of freezing behavior, most labs still score freezing manually or using expensive commercially available software programs that often fail when animals have tethered headmounts.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a limitation of commercial software.

claim: The freezing heuristic had precision of 0.94, recall of 0.87, F1 of 0.91, and specificity of 0.98 on videos of mice wearing patch cords.
source: (D) Performance of freezing heuristic (Precision: 0.94, Recall: 0.87, F1: 0.91, Specificity: 0.98).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3D caption.

claim: Silencing mPFC in previously shocked animals significantly enhanced freezing in the novel context but did not affect freezing in the fear conditioned context.
source: During retrieval sessions, silencing mPFC in previously shocked animals significantly enhanced freezing in the novel context but did not affect freezing in the fear conditioned context (Figure 3F and G).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3F and G with statistical analysis.

claim: mPFC silencing produced a significant decrease in the discrimination index in fear conditioned mice.
source: mPFC silencing thereby produced a significant decrease in the discrimination index in fear conditioned mice (Figure 3H), indicating that mPFC plays a key role in the specificity of recent fear memories.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3H with statistical analysis.

claim: mPFC plays a key role in the specificity of recent fear memories.
source: mPFC silencing thereby produced a significant decrease in the discrimination index in fear conditioned mice (Figure 3H), indicating that mPFC plays a key role in the specificity of recent fear memories.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an interpretation of the data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: BehaviorDEPOT freezing estimates were comparable to a highly trained human rater in the optogenetics experiment.
source: In all analyses, BehaviorDEPOT freezing estimates were comparable to a highly trained human rater (Figure 3F–H).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3F-H.

claim: The BehaviorDEPOT freezing heuristic overcomes a major point of failure in commercially available freezing detection software by maintaining performance levels in videos with visual distractors like a patch cord.
source: By maintaining performance levels even in videos with visual distractors like a patch cord, the BehaviorDEPOT freezing heuristic overcomes a major point of failure in commercially available freezing detection software.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the optogenetics experiment.

claim: Miniature head-mounted microscopes allow imaging of the activity of hundreds of neurons simultaneously in freely moving animals.
source: Miniature head-mounted microscopes now allow us to image the activity of hundreds of neurons simultaneously in freely moving animals (Ghosh et al., 2011; Cai et al., 2016; Shuman et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations.

claim: The MiniCAM is an open-source behavioral imaging platform that natively integrates and synchronizes with open-source UCLA Miniscope hardware and software.
source: The MiniCAM is an open-source behavioral imaging platform that natively integrates and synchronizes with open-source UCLA Miniscope hardware and software (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The MiniCAM uses a 5MP CMOS image sensor with 2592x1944 pixel resolution.
source: The image sensor used is a 5MP CMOS image sensor (MT9P031I12STM-DP, ON Semiconductor) with 2592x1944 pixel resolution and a full resolution frame rate of approximately 14FPS.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the MiniCAM hardware.

claim: The MiniCAM has a full resolution frame rate of approximately 14 FPS.
source: The image sensor used is a 5MP CMOS image sensor (MT9P031I12STM-DP, ON Semiconductor) with 2592x1944 pixel resolution and a full resolution frame rate of approximately 14FPS.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the MiniCAM hardware.

claim: For the PMA application, the MiniCAM's pixels were binned and cropped to achieve 1024x768 pixels at approximately 50FPS.
source: For this application, the MiniCAM's pixels were binned and cropped to achieve 1024x768 pixels at approximately 50FPS.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the MiniCAM configuration.

claim: BehaviorDEPOT freezing ratings for MiniCAM videos were highly consistent with expert human annotations.
source: For these videos, BehaviorDEPOT freezing ratings were highly consistent with expert human annotations (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The freezing heuristic had precision of 0.85, recall of 0.93, F1 of 0.89, and specificity of 0.84 on videos of mice wearing Miniscopes recorded with MiniCAM.
source: (C) Performance of freezing heuristic on videos of mouse wearing Miniscope recorded with MiniCAM (Precision: 0.85; Recall: 0.93; F1 Score: 0.89; Specificity: 0.84).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4C caption.

claim: Nearly half of all neurons in mPFC that exhibited task relevant behavior were specific for either freezing or threat avoidance, or their combination.
source: Nearly half of all neurons that exhibited task relevant behavior and were specific for either freezing or threat avoidance, or their combination (Figure 4L).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4L.

claim: The suite of open-source hardware and software will enable a broader user base to combine Ca2+ imaging with high resolution behavioral analysis.
source: These experiments demonstrate that the BehaviorDEPOT heuristic for detecting freezing is robust across a wide variety of experimental setups with different camera types, keypoint tracking networks, arenas and headmounts. Further, this suite of open-source hardware and software will enable a broader user base to combine Ca2+ imaging with high resolution behavioral analysis.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the Miniscope experiments.

claim: EPM and OFT are used to measure anxiety-related behaviors in the laboratory.
source: EPM and OFT are used to measure anxiety-related behaviors in the laboratory (La-Vu et al., 2020), but these assays are often scored manually or with expensive software such as Ethovision (Noldus et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations.

claim: In the EPM, animals that spend more time in the closed arms are interpreted to have higher anxiety.
source: In the EPM, rodents navigate through an elevated (~1 foot off the ground) plus-shaped maze consisting of two open arms without walls and two enclosed arms with walls. Animals that spend more time in the closed arms are interpreted to have higher anxiety (La-Vu et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a citation.

claim: In the OFT, increased time in the perimeter zone is interpreted as higher anxiety.
source: In the OFT, rodents are placed in an empty arena without a ceiling for 10–15 minutes. Experimenters measure the fraction of time spent in the perimeter of the box vs. the center. Increased time in the perimeter zone is interpreted as higher anxiety.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a description of the OFT assay.

claim: BehaviorDEPOT annotations for EPM were highly consistent with an expert human rater.
source: BehaviorDEPOT annotations were highly consistent with an expert human rater (Figure 5D and E ).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5D and E.

claim: BehaviorDEPOT annotations for OFT were highly consistent with an expert human rater.
source: BehaviorDEPOT annotations were highly consistent with an expert human rater (Figure 5D and E ).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5D and E.

claim: NOE is typically defined as instances when the animal's head is within 2 cm of the object and oriented towards the object.
source: NOE is typically defined as instances when the animal's head is within 2 cm of the object and oriented towards the object (Leger et al., 2013; Vogel-Ciernia and Wood, 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations.

claim: BehaviorDEPOT quantified NOE at levels that were highly consistent with expert human raters.
source: BehaviorDEPOT quantified NOE at levels that were highly consistent with expert human raters (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Effort-based decision-making involves weighing whether it is worth exerting greater effort for a more valuable outcome.
source: For example, effort-based decision-making involves weighing whether it is worth exerting greater effort for a more valuable outcome.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as background on decision-making.

claim: Vicarious trial and error (VTE) is thought to be a marker of deliberative decision-making.
source: However, when reward or effort contingencies are adjusted, animals demonstrate vicarious trial and error (VTE), thought to be a marker of deliberative (rather than habitual) decision-making.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as background on VTE.

claim: Several groups have identified neural signatures of VTE in hippocampus, striatum, and prefrontal cortex.
source: Several groups have identified neural signatures of VTE in hippocampus, striatum, and prefrontal cortex suggesting that animals may be playing out potential choices (i.e. vicariously) based on an internal model of maze contingencies (Redish, 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a citation.

claim: BehaviorDEPOT indicated choice with 100% accuracy in the T-maze task.
source: (D) Automated choice detection using BehaviorDEPOT. BehaviorDEPOT indicated choice with 100% accuracy (FRater(1,6)=6.84, P>0.99, FBarriers(1,7)=4.02, P=0.09; FSubject(6,7)=0.42, P=0.84, two-way ANOVA with Sidak post-hoc comparisons, 84 trials, N=4 mice).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6D caption with statistical analysis.

claim: There was a significant increase in the occurrence of VTE trials when a second barrier was added to the T-maze.
source: We then used our BehaviorDEPOT VTE heuristic to detect the fraction of trials with VTE in T-maze sessions with 1 vs 2 barriers, finding a significant increase in the occurrence of VTE trials when a second barrier was added.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the T-maze experiment.

claim: BehaviorDEPOT VTE detection performance was highly consistent with a human rater.
source: Importantly, the BehaviorDEPOT performance was highly consistent with a human rater (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6F.

claim: The Inter-Rater Module compares annotations from multiple human raters and identifies points of overlap and disagreement.
source: The Inter-Rater Module compares annotations from multiple human raters and identifies points of overlap and disagreement (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The Data Exploration Module helps to identify combinations of keypoint metrics that have high predictive value for behaviors of interest.
source: For users who want to develop new heuristics, the Data Exploration Module helps to identify combinations of keypoint metrics that have high predictive value for behaviors of interest.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the Data Exploration Module.

claim: In focused mode, a generalized linear model (GLM) estimates the likelihood that the behavior is present in a frame across a range of threshold values for two selected metrics.
source: A generalized linear model (GLM) also estimates the likelihood that the behavior is present in a frame across a range of threshold values for the two selected metrics (Figure 8A), allowing users to optimize parameters in combination.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 8A.

claim: In broad mode, the Data Exploration Module uses all available keypoint metrics to generate a GLM that can predict behavior.
source: In broad mode, the module uses all available keypoint metrics to generate a GLM that can predict behavior as well as a rank-order list of metrics based on their predictive weights.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the Data Exploration Module.

claim: The linear velocity of the back and angular velocity of the head tracked particularly well with freezing.
source: Indeed, we discovered that the linear velocity of the back and angular velocity of the head tracked particularly well with freezing (Figure 8B and C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 8B and C.

claim: A major advantage of using heuristics to detect behaviors is that parameters can be quickly and easily tuned to optimize behavioral detection in out-of-sample data.
source: A major advantage of using heuristics to detect behaviors is that parameters can be quickly and easily tuned to optimize behavioral detection in out-of-sample data.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an advantage of the heuristic approach.

claim: The Optimization Module identifies the set of thresholds that maximize detection accuracy by sweeping through the parameter space for chosen metrics.
source: By sweeping through the parameter space for chosen metrics, the Optimization Module identifies the set of thresholds that maximize detection accuracy (Figure 9A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 9A.

claim: The optimal combination of thresholds for rat videos achieved F1 scores greater than 0.9.
source: In both cases, the optimal combination of thresholds for each video set (Figure 9C and D) achieved high F1 scores (>0.9), indicating that our chosen features for freezing detection are robust across a range of cameras, keypoint tracking networks, experimental conditions, and rodent species.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 9C and D.

claim: The optimal combination of thresholds for mouse videos achieved F1 scores greater than 0.9.
source: In both cases, the optimal combination of thresholds for each video set (Figure 9C and D) achieved high F1 scores (>0.9), indicating that our chosen features for freezing detection are robust across a range of cameras, keypoint tracking networks, experimental conditions, and rodent species.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 9C and D.

claim: The chosen features for freezing detection are robust across a range of cameras, keypoint tracking networks, experimental conditions, and rodent species.
source: In both cases, the optimal combination of thresholds for each video set (Figure 9C and D) achieved high F1 scores (>0.9), indicating that our chosen features for freezing detection are robust across a range of cameras, keypoint tracking networks, experimental conditions, and rodent species.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the optimization experiments.

claim: The BehaviorDEPOT freezing heuristic performed robustly on videos of rats recorded in a different lab with precision of 0.93, recall of 0.88, F1 of 0.91, and specificity of 0.96.
source: (F) The BehaviorDEPOT heuristic performed robustly on videos of rats recorded in a different lab (Precision = 0.93; Recall = 0.88; F1=0.91; Specificity = 0.96). BehaviorDEPOT freezing detection was comparable to highly trained human raters (N=4 videos, P=0.89, Mann-Whitney U).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 9F caption with statistical analysis.

claim: The BehaviorDEPOT freezing heuristic performed robustly on videos of mice recorded in a different lab with precision of 0.98, recall of 0.92, F1 of 0.95, and specificity of 0.95.
source: (G) The BehaviorDEPOT heuristic performed robustly on videos of mice recorded in a different lab (Precision = 0.98; Recall = 0.92; F1=0.95; Specificity = 0.95). BehaviorDEPOT freezing detection was comparable to highly trained human raters (N=4 videos, P=0.49, Mann-Whitney U).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 9G caption with statistical analysis.

claim: JAABA is geared toward a non-coding audience.
source: Like BehaviorDEPOT, JAABA is geared toward a non-coding audience and its classifiers are based on an intuitive understanding of what defines behaviors.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section comparing BehaviorDEPOT to JAABA.

claim: JAABA has been widely adopted by the Drosophila community with great success.
source: JAABA uses supervised machine learning to detect behaviors and has been widely adopted by the Drosophila community with great success.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section comparing BehaviorDEPOT to JAABA.

claim: Fewer studies have used JAABA to study rodents.
source: However, fewer studies have used JAABA to study rodents, suggesting there may be some challenges associated with using JAABA for rodent behavioral assays.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section comparing BehaviorDEPOT to JAABA.

claim: MoTr and Ctrax performed poorly when rodents were in fear conditioning chambers which have high-contrast bars on the floor.
source: The segmentation algorithms performed poorly when rodents were in fear conditioning chambers which have high-contrast bars on the floor but could fit ellipses to mice in an open field, in which the mouse is small relative to the environment and runs against a clean white background (Figure 10A–B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 10A-B.

claim: MoTr and Ctrax could fit ellipses to mice in an open field.
source: The segmentation algorithms performed poorly when rodents were in fear conditioning chambers which have high-contrast bars on the floor but could fit ellipses to mice in an open field, in which the mouse is small relative to the environment and runs against a clean white background (Figure 10A–B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 10A-B.

claim: The BehaviorDEPOT heuristic for freezing had significantly higher recall and F1 scores than JAABA when tested on a separate set of videos.
source: Even when we gave JAABA more training data than we used to develop BehaviorDEPOT heuristics (6 videos vs. 3 videos), the BehaviorDEPOT heuristic for freezing had significantly higher recall and F1 scores when tested on a separate set of videos (Figure 10D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 10D with statistical analysis.

claim: JAABA could not distinguish VTE vs. non-VTE trials and labeled every trial as containing VTE.
source: When we tested its performance on a separate set of videos, JAABA could not distinguish VTE vs. non-VTE trials. It labeled every trial as containing VTE (Figure 10E), suggesting a well-fit ellipse is not sufficient to detect these fine angular head movements.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 10E.

claim: A well-fit ellipse is not sufficient to detect fine angular head movements like VTE.
source: When we tested its performance on a separate set of videos, JAABA could not distinguish VTE vs. non-VTE trials. It labeled every trial as containing VTE (Figure 10E), suggesting a well-fit ellipse is not sufficient to detect these fine angular head movements.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an interpretation of the JAABA VTE results.

claim: BehaviorDEPOT can quantify behaviors with reference to spatial or temporal cues of interest.
source: Another strength of BehaviorDEPOT relative to JAABA is that BehaviorDEPOT can quantify behaviors with reference to spatial or temporal cues of interest.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an advantage of BehaviorDEPOT over JAABA.

claim: Keypoint tracking algorithms and in vivo methods including optogenetics, fiber photometry, and miniscope recordings have become increasingly accessible and widely adopted.
source: Keypoint tracking algorithms and in vivo methods including optogenetics, fiber photometry, and miniscope recordings have become increasingly accessible and widely adopted.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as context for the development of BehaviorDEPOT.

claim: BehaviorDEPOT's graphical interface allows even inexperienced coders to run experiments, automatically detect behaviors, and analyze the results of popular assays.
source: BehaviorDEPOT is a general utility behavioral analysis software package based on keypoint tracking. Its graphical interface allows even inexperienced coders to run experiments, automatically detect behaviors, and analyze the results of popular assays including those run in operant chambers (e.g. fear conditioning) or spatial mazes (e.g. T-mazes or elevated plus mazes).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a summary of BehaviorDEPOT's capabilities.

claim: BehaviorDEPOT's built-in heuristic freezing detector has low error rates across a range of video recording setups.
source: Our built-in heuristic freezing detector has low error rates across a range of video recording setups, including videos of both mice and rats wearing tethered headmounts.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a summary of the freezing heuristic performance.

claim: BehaviorDEPOT builds rich data structures that facilitate alignment of neural and behavioral data.
source: It also builds rich data structures that facilitate alignment of neural and behavioral data, and we provide additional code in our GitHub repository for this purpose.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a feature of BehaviorDEPOT.

claim: The experiment module and the UCLA MiniCAM extend the utility of BehaviorDEPOT, together forming a fully open-source pipeline from data collection to analysis.
source: The experiment module and the UCLA MiniCAM extend the utility of BehaviorDEPOT, together forming a fully open-source pipeline from data collection to analysis.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a summary of the complete pipeline.

claim: BehaviorDEPOT employs heuristics to measure human-defined behaviors based on keypoint tracking data.
source: BehaviorDEPOT employs heuristics to measure human-defined behaviors based on keypoint tracking data.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion describing the approach.

claim: Keypoints can be used to simultaneously track location and classify fine-scale behaviors.
source: Keypoints can be used to simultaneously track location and classify fine-scale behaviors.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an advantage of keypoint tracking.

claim: Keypoint tracking is well suited for analysis of widely-used assays in which researchers have carefully defined behaviors based on the pose of the animal and its location in an arena.
source: As such, keypoint tracking is well suited for analysis of widely-used assays in which researchers have carefully defined behaviors based on the pose of the animal and its location in an arena.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a rationale for using keypoint tracking.

claim: Assays including fear conditioning, avoidance, T-mazes, and elevated plus mazes are published in tens of thousands of studies each year.
source: Assays including fear conditioning, avoidance, T-mazes, and elevated plus mazes are published in tens of thousands of studies each year.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as context for the importance of BehaviorDEPOT.

claim: Most labs still rely on laborious manual annotation, expensive commercial software packages, or open-source software packages that can fail to detect fine movements for behavioral analysis.
source: Yet most still rely on laborious manual annotation, expensive commercial software packages, or open-source software packages that can fail to detect fine movements and are error prone, especially in visually complex arenas.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a problem in the field.

claim: BehaviorDEPOT's heuristics are easier to interpret than methods that use supervised machine learning.
source: In contrast to methods that use supervised machine learning (Nilsson et al., 2020; Segalin et al., 2021; Hong et al., 2015; Bohnslav et al., 2021), BehaviorDEPOT's heuristics are easier to interpret and can be easily tweaked to fit out-of-sample videos.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an advantage of BehaviorDEPOT over machine learning methods.

claim: BehaviorDEPOT heuristics can be easily tweaked to fit out-of-sample videos.
source: In contrast to methods that use supervised machine learning (Nilsson et al., 2020; Segalin et al., 2021; Hong et al., 2015; Bohnslav et al., 2021), BehaviorDEPOT's heuristics are easier to interpret and can be easily tweaked to fit out-of-sample videos.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an advantage of BehaviorDEPOT.

claim: The automation of BehaviorDEPOT serves to standardize human-expert definitions and can enhance rigor and reproducibility.
source: However, the automation serves to standardize human-expert definitions and can enhance rigor and reproducibility.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an advantage of automation.

claim: When behaviors are clearly defined, developing reliable BehaviorDEPOT heuristics may require less human-labeled data compared to a supervised machine learning approach.
source: Moreover, when behaviors are clearly defined, developing reliable BehaviorDEPOT heuristics may require less human-labeled data compared to a supervised machine learning approach.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an advantage of the heuristic approach.

claim: Programs like B-SOiD and MotionMapper are geared toward analysis of even more subtle behaviors that are more challenging for humans to reliably label.
source: Other methods use unsupervised approaches to classify behavior based on keypoint tracking. While relatively free of human biases, programs like B-SOiD (Hsu and Yttri, 2021) and MotionMapper (Mathis, 2022) are geared toward analysis of even more subtle behaviors that are more challenging for humans to reliably label and may be out of reach technically for researchers that lack computational expertise.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion comparing BehaviorDEPOT to unsupervised methods.

claim: The graphical interface and intuitive design of BehaviorDEPOT heuristics ensure it will serve a broad audience.
source: The graphical interface and intuitive design of BehaviorDEPOT heuristics ensure it will serve a broad audience.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a conclusion about BehaviorDEPOT's accessibility.

claim: BehaviorDEPOT requires users to first train keypoint tracking models.
source: BehaviorDEPOT does require users to first train keypoint tracking models.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a requirement for using BehaviorDEPOT.

claim: The accuracy, precision, and flexibility achieved by keypoint tracking methods will make BehaviorDEPOT more broadly useful than classifiers based on more coarse detection methods.
source: However, the accuracy, precision, and flexibility achieved by these methods will make BehaviorDEPOT more broadly useful than classifiers based on more coarse detection methods (e.g. background subtraction) that are not robust to environmental complexity or subject appearance.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an advantage of keypoint tracking.

claim: Some freezing detectors use pixel change functions to detect periods of no movement and can operate in complex arenas like fear conditioning chambers.
source: Some freezing detectors use pixel change functions to detect periods of no movement and can operate in complex arenas like fear conditioning chambers.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion describing other freezing detection methods.

claim: Pixel change-based freezing detectors often fail to detect freezing when animals are wearing head-mounts for optogenetics or neural recordings because tethered patch cords can move even when the animal is immobile.
source: However, they often fail to detect freezing when animals are wearing head-mounts for optogenetics or neural recordings because tethered patch cords can move even when the animal is immobile.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a limitation of pixel change-based methods.

claim: ezTrack, VideoFreeze, and ANYmaze allow researchers to crop the tether out of the video, but this requires side-view videos and thereby constrains concurrent spatial analyses.
source: To circumvent this problem, ezTrack (Pennington et al., 2019), VideoFreeze (Anagnostaras et al., 2010), and ANYmaze allow researchers to crop the tether out of the video, but this requires side-view videos and thereby constrains concurrent spatial analyses.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citations describing limitations of other methods.

claim: With keypoint tracking, researchers can track body parts that best fit their experimental design and can detect fine movements of individual body parts.
source: With keypoint tracking, researchers can track body parts that best fit their experimental design and can detect fine movements of individual body parts, allowing researchers to detect a wider array of behaviors and discover subtle phenotypes arising from manipulations.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an advantage of keypoint tracking.

claim: An important step in supervised behavior classification is establishing a ground truth definition of behavior.
source: An important step in supervised behavior classification is establishing a ground truth definition of behavior.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as background on supervised classification.

claim: MARS includes a large dataset of human annotations for social behaviors and provides detailed quantitative descriptions of similarity and divergence between human raters.
source: MARS includes a large dataset of human annotations for social behaviors and provides detailed quantitative descriptions of similarity and divergence between human raters (Segalin et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with a citation.

claim: The BehaviorDEPOT Inter-Rater Module has added functions to automatically calculate performance statistics with the click of a button.
source: While the MARS BENTO feature can import human annotations for visualization alongside behavior videos or automated annotations, our Inter-Rater Module has added functions to automatically calculate performance statistics with the click of a button.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an advantage of BehaviorDEPOT's Inter-Rater Module.

claim: The BehaviorDEPOT heuristic for freezing detection operates on similar principles to commercial software that apply a motion threshold and a minimum duration threshold.
source: Our heuristic for freezing detection operates on similar principles to commercial software that apply a motion threshold and a minimum duration threshold to detect bouts of freezing.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion comparing BehaviorDEPOT to commercial software.

claim: BehaviorDEPOT has added functionality in that freezing detection can be integrated with spatial analyses.
source: However, BehaviorDEPOT has added functionality in that freezing detection can be integrated with spatial analyses so researchers can determine not only when an animal is freezing, but also where it is freezing.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an advantage of BehaviorDEPOT.

claim: Commercial freezing detection algorithms are not well validated.
source: Another major limitation of commercial algorithms is that they are not well validated (Anagnostaras et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with a citation.

claim: Researchers typically use their intuition to set thresholds for freezing in commercial software.
source: Researchers typically use their intuition to set thresholds for freezing.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a limitation of current practices.

claim: BehaviorDEPOT's Optimization Module allows users to adjust parameters and determine the combination of thresholds that produce the lowest error rates.
source: BehaviorDEPOT's Optimization Module allows users to adjust parameters and determine the combination of thresholds that produce the lowest error rates.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a feature of BehaviorDEPOT.

claim: By making the optimization and validation process easy, BehaviorDEPOT will enhance the rigor of behavior classification and increase reproducibility across labs.
source: By making the optimization and validation process easy – it can be done with a few button clicks in the graphical interface – BehaviorDEPOT will enhance the rigor of behavior classification and increase reproducibility across labs.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a conclusion about BehaviorDEPOT's impact.

claim: Female and male C57B1/6 J mice aged 10–16 weeks were used in the experiments.
source: Female and male C57B1/6 J mice (JAX Stock No. 000664) aged 10–16 weeks were group housed (2–5 per cage) and kept on a 12 hr light cycle.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Mice were group housed (2–5 per cage) and kept on a 12 hr light cycle.
source: Female and male C57B1/6 J mice (JAX Stock No. 000664) aged 10–16 weeks were group housed (2–5 per cage) and kept on a 12 hr light cycle.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Following behavior conditioning, animals were individually housed until the memory retrieval sessions.
source: Following behavior conditioning, animals were individually housed until the memory retrieval sessions.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: All animal procedures followed animal care guidelines approved by the University of California, Los Angeles Chancellor's Animal Research Committee.
source: All animal procedures followed animal care guidelines approved by the University of California, Los Angeles Chancellor's Animal Research Committee.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Mice were handled for 5 days preceding the behavioral testing procedure.
source: Mice were handled for 5 days preceding the behavioral testing procedure.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section describing the contextual fear conditioning protocol.

claim: During contextual fear conditioning, mice received five 0.75mA footshocks spaced 1 min apart after a 2-min baseline period.
source: Mice were placed in the chamber and then after a 2-min baseline period, received five 0.75mA footshocks spaced 1 min apart.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section describing the contextual fear conditioning protocol.

claim: AAV1-syn-jGCaMP7f.WPRE was purchased from Addgene and diluted to a working titer of 8.5x1012 GC/ml.
source: AAV1-syn-jGCaMP7f.WPRE (ItemID: 104488-AAV1) was purchased from Addgene and diluted to a working titer of 8.5x1012 GC/ml.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: AAV1-CamKIIa-stGtACR2-FusionRed was purchased from Addgene and diluted to a working titer of 9.5x1011 GC/ml.
source: AAV1-CamKIIa-stGtACR2-FusionRed (ItemID: 105669-AAV1) was purchased from Addgene and diluted to a working titer of 9.5x1011 GC/ml.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: 400 nL of AAV was pressure injected into each site in mPFC at 100 nL/min.
source: A Hamilton syringe containing AAV1-CaMKIIa-stGtACR2-WPRE was lowered into the burr hole and 400 nL of AAV was pressure injected into each site (DV –2.25 mm and –2.50 mm from bregma) at 100 nL/min using a microinjector (WPI, UMP3T-1).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section describing the AAV injection procedure.

claim: Carprofen (5 mg/kg) was administered both during surgery and for 2 days after surgery.
source: Carprofen (5 mg/kg) was administered both during surgery and for 2 days after surgery together with amoxicillin (0.25 mg/mL) in the drinking water for 7 days after surgery.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section describing post-surgical care.

claim: Amoxicillin (0.25 mg/mL) was administered in the drinking water for 7 days after surgery.
source: Carprofen (5 mg/kg) was administered both during surgery and for 2 days after surgery together with amoxicillin (0.25 mg/mL) in the drinking water for 7 days after surgery.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section describing post-surgical care.

claim: Animals were habituated to the patch-cord for 3 days in advance of optogenetic stimulation.
source: Animals were habituated to the patch-cord for 3 days in advance of optogenetic stimulation.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section describing the optogenetics protocol.

claim: Optical stimulation was delivered continuously with 2.5 mW power at the fiber tip.
source: Stimulation was delivered continuously with 2.5 mW power at the fiber tip.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section describing the optogenetics protocol.

claim: MIN1PIPE was used to extract and process neural signals from mPFC neurons.
source: Using MIN1PIPE (Lu et al., 2018), we extracted and processed neural signals from 513 mPFC neurons across 3 mice.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section with a citation.

claim: 513 mPFC neurons were recorded across 3 mice during the PMA retrieval session.
source: Using MIN1PIPE (Lu et al., 2018), we extracted and processed neural signals from 513 mPFC neurons across 3 mice.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Neurons were considered significantly activated during a behavior if their AUC was greater than 97.5% of AUCs in the null distributions.
source: Neurons were considered significantly activated during a behavior if their AUC was greater than 97.5% of AUCs in the null distributions and significantly suppressed if their AUC value was in the lowest 2.5% of all AUCs in the null distribution.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section describing the analysis of neural data.

claim: Neurons were considered significantly suppressed during a behavior if their AUC value was in the lowest 2.5% of all AUCs in the null distribution.
source: Neurons were considered significantly activated during a behavior if their AUC was greater than 97.5% of AUCs in the null distributions and significantly suppressed if their AUC value was in the lowest 2.5% of all AUCs in the null distribution.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section describing the analysis of neural data.

claim: Freezing was defined as the absence of movement except for respiration in manual annotations.
source: Freezing was defined as the absence of movement except for respiration.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section describing manual annotation criteria.

claim: Novel object exploration was defined as when the mouse's head was oriented toward the object with the nose within 2 cm of the object.
source: Novel object exploration was defined as when the mouse's head was oriented toward the object with the nose within 2 cm of the object.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section describing manual annotation criteria.

claim: VTE was defined as when the animal was in the choice zone and swept its head back and forth across approximately 180 degrees.
source: VTE was defined as when the animal was in the choice zone and swept its head back and forth across ~180°.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section describing manual annotation criteria.

claim: Videos were randomly assigned to heuristic development and test sets to ensure that highly correlated temporally adjacent frames are not sorted into training and test sets.
source: To develop heuristics, videos were randomly assigned to heuristic development and test sets. Dividing up the dataset by video rather than by frame ensures that highly correlated temporally adjacent frames are not sorted into training and test sets, which can cause overestimation of accuracy.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section describing the heuristic development methodology.

claim: The default minimum duration threshold for freezing bouts is 0.9 s.
source: Finally, the heuristic rejects freezing bouts that are shorter than a user-defined minimum duration. The default value is 0.9 s, a definition that draws on published literature (Anagnostaras et al., 2000) and was tested empirically to give the most cohesiveness with human raters.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section with a citation.

claim: The default back velocity threshold for the freezing heuristic is 0.59 cm/s.
source: This heuristic imports the Metrics structure and identifies frames in which the linear velocity of the back is below a specified threshold value (default is 0.59 cm/s) and angular velocity of the head is below a specified threshold value (default is 15 deg/s).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section describing the velocity-based freezing heuristic.

claim: The default head angular velocity threshold for the freezing heuristic is 15 deg/s.
source: This heuristic imports the Metrics structure and identifies frames in which the linear velocity of the back is below a specified threshold value (default is 0.59 cm/s) and angular velocity of the head is below a specified threshold value (default is 15 deg/s).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section describing the velocity-based freezing heuristic.
